strengths: Comprehensive experimental design: multiple model scales (400M, 1.4B), multiple strong baselines (WRAP, ProX, ReWire), token-budget sweeps, component ablations, reward-dynamics analyses, and efficiency comparisons (36.7× speedup over ReWire).

The ablation of reward functions is informative: showing that faithfulness rewards are necessary (RL w/o Faithfulness drops Core score) and that alternative quality rewards (DCLM-fastText, data influence) are hacked or unoptimizable is a genuinely useful negative result for future RL-for-data work.
Distributional and case-study analyses (Figures 6–7, Appendix C) go beyond headline scores and substantiate the 'faithful recycling' claim qualitatively.
Reasonable reproducibility: hyperparameters, prompts, thresholds, and inference details are documented, and the authors state they will release code, rephraser, and data.
weaknesses: No statistical rigor around the headline claims. The 1.4B gain is only +0.0135 Core score (0.28578 → 0.29929), averaged over 22 tasks from single pretraining runs with no seeds, error bars, or significance tests. At this margin, run-to-run variance in small-scale pretraining is a real concern, yet '4.7%–14.0% relative improvement' is stated as established fact.

Evaluation circularity: DataMan is both the RL quality reward and the metric used to demonstrate data-quality improvements (Figure 6a, Figure 8, 'Score of 5 from 20% to 60%'). Reward–metric coincidence makes these analyses uninformative about genuine quality gains; the paper acknowledges reward hacking for other metrics but does not confront the same risk for its own chosen reward.

Internal inconsistency in the scaling story: Figure 3 appears to show RePro at B=28.8B (0.267) scoring below the organic baseline (0.283), which contradicts the text's claim that RePro 'consistently outperforms the organic-only baseline across different B.' The '2–3× organic data efficiency' claim rests on cherry-picked operating points, and the drop is explained away rather than investigated.

Baseline fairness is shaky: ReWire is reimplemented from a 7.2B subsample of its released data (authors admit a possible advantage to ReWire), and concurrent methods (RefineX, BeyondWeb) are omitted entirely, so the 'outperforms SOTA' claim is narrow.

Faithfulness rewards are coarse heuristics (binary BERTScore threshold at 0.65, an LLM binary structure judge, a hard length cap), with coefficients (3,1,1,1) chosen ad hoc; robustness of conclusions to these design choices is not established beyond one coefficient sweep for DataMan.

Duplication risk is underexamined: recycling paraphrases of the same organic documents effectively upweights near-duplicate content within the training set; the paper does not analyze similarity between organic and recycled shards or implications for memorization.
Scale and generality gap: all conclusions come from ≤1.4B models and ≤28.8B tokens on DCLM-RefinedWeb only, while the framing targets frontier 'data wall' scaling; extrapolation is speculative.

No limitations or ethics discussion in the manuscript. Training a model to paraphrase web text at scale raises copyright/consent concerns (paraphrasing can be used to launder protected content), and this is never addressed.

strengths: Comprehensive and well-structured experimental design: the paper evaluates at two pretraining scales (400M and 1.4B), across 22 downstream tasks, against multiple strong baselines (organic-only, WRAP, ProX, ReWire), which directly supports the central claim that RL-trained small rephrasers can outperform prompting-based 70B recycling.

The reward design (one quality + three faithfulness rewards) is well motivated and empirically dissected: Figure 4 (reward dynamics with/without faithfulness constraints), Figure 5 (reward hacking of fastText and influence rewards), and Figure 6 (distributional analyses of DataMan score, BERTScore, structure, and length) collectively provide convincing evidence that each reward component does what it claims.

Section 5.3 is a genuinely valuable contribution beyond the main method: demonstrating that commonly used quality metrics (n-gram classifiers, data influence) are vulnerable to reward hacking or unoptimizable is an insight useful to anyone doing RL on text generation with proxy quality rewards.
The ablation in Table 3 cleanly separates prompting, SFT, RL without faithfulness, and full RL, establishing that RL with faithful rewards (not just a stronger prior) drives the gains.
Strong reproducibility: hyperparameters for all models (Table 7), all prompts (Appendix B.5), evaluation task/shot details (Table 6), and a commitment to release code, rephraser, and recycled data.

The paper treats baselines fairly and transparently, e.g., explicitly noting in B.2 that their ReWire reproduction uses a larger effective pool, and excluding unstable tasks (CommonsenseQA) with justification.
Efficiency analysis (Table 4) quantifies the practical advantage (36.7x speedup over ReWire), substantiating the cost-effectiveness claim rather than leaving it implicit.
weaknesses: No statistical significance reporting: pretraining runs have no seeds/error bars, and at the 1.4B scale the gap between RePro (0.29929) and ProX (0.29186) or ReWire (0.29029) is fairly small; without variance estimates, the 1.4B results are less compelling than the 400M results.

Some circularity between reward and evaluation: DataMan serves both as the RL quality reward and as a headline evaluation metric (Figures 6a and 8), so improvements on those plots are partially self-fulfilling; the downstream Core score mitigates this, but the paper could more explicitly de-emphasize DataMan-based evaluation.

Faithfulness claims lean on LLM judges (BERTScore threshold, a prompted structural comparison model, Gemini 2.5 Flash-Lite for structure type and key-point recall in Figure 1b), which are themselves imperfect validators; the key-point recall analysis would benefit from human verification on a small sample.

Generalization to frontier scales is untested: all pretraining is at 400M/1.4B on DCLM with 28.8B tokens; the paper argues the data wall motivates the method for frontier models, but a stronger acknowledgment of this scale limitation (e.g., in a limitations section) would be appropriate.

The relative gains are sensitive to the token budget B (Figure 3 shows a drop at B=28.8B), so the 2-3x organic data efficiency claim holds in a specific regime rather than universally; the mechanism behind the drop deserves more analysis.

Minor presentation issues: the text says DataMan uses '13 criteria' while the prompt lists 14; the abstract cites wide relative gain ranges (4.7%-14.0%) without immediately clarifying they span two model scales.

strengths: The central idea is compelling and well-executed: using RL (GRPO) to train a small (1B-4B) rephraser with a quality reward (DataMan) plus explicit faithfulness rewards (BERTScore, structure, length), yielding a rephraser that roughly matches or beats prompting a 70B model while being up to ~87x cheaper in rephrasing compute (Table 4, B.1).

The evaluation is unusually rigorous for this area: three model scales (400M/1.4B/2.8B), 22 downstream tasks, a compute-equalized organic baseline (Table 5) ruling out 'more FLOPs' as the explanation, a seed-variance analysis (Table 8) showing gains exceed 2x the noise floor, and a controlled ReWire comparison on matched organic pools and matched rephraser models (Table 7) that removes a significant confound from the headline claim.

Ablations are thorough and informative: each faithfulness reward is removed individually with both downstream and distributional consequences shown (Figures 6-7), a strengthened prompting/SFT baseline with reward descriptions is included (Prompting+, SFT+), the 'No Recycling from D_org-hq' experiment isolates gains from non-high-quality data, and the fastText/influence quality-reward study (B.7, Figure 10) candidly documents reward hacking, which strengthens the justification for DataMan.

The faithfulness analyses (key-point support/omit/contradict ratios in Figure 1b, operation taxonomy in Figure 5, qualitative case studies in Appendix D) directly substantiate the paper's framing that recycling should preserve organic characteristics, connecting the method to the model-collapse literature rather than just chasing benchmark scores.

Honest and detailed treatment of limitations: unavailability of ReWire's exact pool, single-seed RL pipeline reruns, corpus-specificity (DCLM/English Common Crawl), and non-open-sourced concurrent baselines are all explicitly discussed; hyperparameters and prompts are provided, and code is released, supporting reproducibility.
weaknesses: Absolute gains are modest (Core score improvements of ~0.02-0.03, i.e., 3.7%-14.5% relative), and while the paper shows these exceed seed variance for the organic baseline, the RL/recycling pipeline itself was not re-run across seeds, so the full end-to-end variance of RePro is not directly quantified (acknowledged in B.4).

All main experiments use a single corpus (DCLM-RefinedWeb) and English text; the claimed generality of the recycling approach across corpora (FineWeb, RedPajama) is deferred to future work, limiting the reach of the conclusions.

The quality reward depends on DataMan, an LLM-as-a-judge metric; although the paper shows fastText and influence rewards fail and analyzes all 13 DataMan criteria, the possibility of optimizing toward DataMan's specific biases (and a resulting train/test circularity with data-selection practice) is not fully resolved.

The connection between faithfulness rewards and avoiding model collapse is argued qualitatively and via proxy analyses (key-point recall, distribution matching); no actual recursive/iterative recycling or collapse-stress experiments are performed, so this motivation remains partially supported.

Some design choices appear tuned on relatively small validation sets (e.g., 128-sample validation rewards, thresholds like tau_BERTScore=0.65 derived from distributional observations), and the sensitivity of final downstream results to the reward-weighting coefficients is studied only via reward curves rather than downstream accuracy.

strengths: The core idea is well-motivated and timely: training a small (1B–4B) rephraser with RL to convert low-quality web data into high-quality pretraining tokens, rather than prompting a 70B model, addresses both the compute cost and faithfulness limitations of prior recycling methods (WRAP, ReWire, ProX).

The experimental evidence is unusually thorough for this area: three model scales (400M/1.4B/2.8B), multiple unique-token budgets, a compute-equalized organic baseline (Table 5) that rules out the 'more compute' confound, controlled comparisons with ReWire on matched organic pools (Table 7), and a noise-floor significance analysis with multiple seeds (Table 8).

The reward design is sensible and the ablations are convincing: Table 3 and Figure 7 show that faithfulness rewards are necessary (without them the rephraser drifts, BERTScore/structure/length rewards collapse, and downstream performance drops), and the 'No Recycling from D_org-hq' ablation shows 77.2% of gains come from genuinely low-quality data rather than re-deriving high-quality data.

The faithfulness analysis (key-point support/omit/contradict ratios in Figure 1b, fastText quality-transition analysis in Figure 4, structural and length distribution matching in Figure 6) directly substantiates the central claim that recycling is faithful rather than just quality-maximizing, and the finding that 63.5% of high-quality recycled data originates from low-quality organic data is a valuable insight.

The appendix is candid and adds real substance: the fastText reward-hacking case study (B.7), the observation that DataMan selection does not transfer to rephraser RL reward, and the honest statement that the full pipeline was not re-run across seeds due to compute constraints.
Reproducibility is good: prompts, hyperparameters, reward thresholds, and implementation details are all provided, and code is stated to be released.
weaknesses: There is a potential circularity concern around DataMan: it is used both as the RL quality reward and as the quality function for filtering/selecting the final corpus, and DataMan is itself an LLM-judge whose correlation with true pretraining value is asserted rather than established. The fastText comparison (B.7) partially mitigates this, but the paper would benefit from an independent downstream-motivated quality metric.

All main results are on a single corpus (DCLM-RefinedWeb); the authors acknowledge extensions to FineWeb/RedPajama as future work. Generalization of the conclusion across data distributions remains unverified.

Most headline comparisons (Table 2, Table 3) appear to be single-seed runs; the multi-seed analysis covers only the organic baseline, and the absolute gains are small in magnitude (e.g., Core 0.18990 → 0.21749 at 400M), so seed noise on the REPRO side cannot be fully ruled out even though gains exceed 2x the organic-side std.
The structure reward relies on an in-context LLM judge (Qwen3-4B prompted for structure comparison), which is a noisy, uncalibrated binary signal; no validation of this judge's accuracy is reported.
The optional GPT-4o SFT stage introduces a proprietary teacher, and the interaction between SFT and RL (SFT hurts Core score, and the authors' explanation is speculative) is not fully understood.
Comparison with concurrent methods like RefineX is deferred, though the authors give a reasonable justification (code/data not released).
